lesson.title: Passing the Mail: How SMTP Moves a Message Toward Its Destination
lesson.summary: SMTP is the application layer protocol responsible for sending and relaying email from a sender's mail server toward the recipient's mail server, defined in an open RFC standard and built on top of TCP's reliable delivery.
lesson.body:
SMTP, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, is the protocol that moves an email message from the point it is sent toward the mailbox where it will eventually be read. It sits at the application layer, meaning it defines a set of commands and responses that make sense to email software, and it relies on TCP underneath to actually get those commands and the message bytes across the network reliably and in order, which matters a great deal for something like an email message, since a corrupted or reordered message is not something a user can tolerate the way a dropped video frame might be tolerable. SMTP itself is defined in an RFC, an open, versioned standard document, which is exactly the kind of specification that lets independently written mail server software from different vendors all interoperate correctly.

An email's journey from sender to recipient usually involves more than one hop. A user's mail program submits an outgoing message to their provider's outgoing mail server, which acts as a relay: it uses SMTP to hand the message off to the recipient's mail server, and depending on the mail infrastructure involved, that handoff might actually pass through more than one intermediate server before reaching its final destination. Each of these hops is a separate SMTP conversation between two servers. Traditionally SMTP relay traffic between mail servers uses TCP port 25, while a mail client submitting a new outgoing message to its own provider typically uses port 587 with authentication and encryption, a distinction that exists because open, unauthenticated relaying on port 25 became a major source of spam.

SMTP is a text based, command and response protocol, which makes an actual conversation readable. A simplified exchange looks like this: the client opens the connection and identifies itself with EHLO and its domain name; issues MAIL FROM:<alice@example.com> to declare the sender; issues RCPT TO:<bob@example.org> to declare the recipient; sends DATA followed by the message headers and body, ending with a line containing just a period; and finally sends QUIT to close the session. At each step the server responds with a numeric reply code, similar in spirit to HTTP status codes but from a separate numbering scheme, such as 250 for a successful step or 550 if, for example, the mailbox does not exist.

It is important to be precise about what SMTP actually does and does not do. SMTP is a push protocol: it moves a message from a sender toward a recipient's mail server and deposits it into a mailbox there. It has nothing to do with how the recipient later reads that message. Once the message is sitting in the recipient's mailbox on their provider's server, the recipient's own device needs a completely different kind of protocol to fetch and view it, which is exactly the gap that the next two protocols, IMAP and POP3, exist to fill.
